content: 1. The eggs of Capillaria hepatica are observed in liver tissue stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). The image highlights the eggs within the liver tissue, adapted from CDC resources. 2. A cross-section of Capillaria hepatica in liver tissue stained with H&E shows the presence of a stichocyte (indicated by a black arrow) and bacillary bands (indicated by blue arrows). The image was captured at 200x magnification and adapted from CDC materials. 3. An adult Heterophyes heterophyes fluke stained with carmine is shown. The labeled structures include the oral sucker (OS), pharynx (PH), intestine (IN), ventral sucker or acetabulum (AC), and eggs within the uterus (UT). This image is adapted from CDC resources. 4. The intermediate host of Heterophyes heterophyes, Cerithideopsilla cingulata, is depicted. This snail species is found in Southeast Asia. The image is courtesy of Conchology, Inc., Mactan Island, Philippines, and adapted from CDC. 5. The egg of Hymenolepis diminuta is shown in an unstained wet mount of concentrated stool. The image was captured at 400x magnification and adapted from CDC resources. 6. Proglottids of Hymenolepis diminuta stained with carmine are shown. The proglottids exhibit a craspedote form. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 7. The egg of Hymenolepis nana is observed in an unstained wet mount. The polar filaments between the oncosphere and the outer shell are clearly visible. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 8. A trichrome-stained stool specimen shows the egg of Hymenolepis nana. Although trichrome is not the preferred method for observing helminth eggs, they can still be detected. The eggs appear distorted, likely due to the use of zinc polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) for preservation. The image is courtesy of the Oregon State Public Health Laboratory and adapted from CDC. 9. A higher magnification (1000x, oil) of Hymenolepis nana eggs shows hooks that do not stain with H&E but are refractile and visible with proper microscope adjustments. Polar filaments are visible in the egg in the upper right quadrant of the image. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 10. A higher magnification of the scolex of Hymenolepis nana adults shows two suckers and rostellar hooks clearly. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 11. A cyst of Entamoeba coli is shown in a concentrated wet mount stained with iodine. Five nuclei are visible in this focal plane. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 12. A mature cyst of Entamoeba coli stained with trichrome is shown. The same cyst is depicted in two different focal planes, revealing eight nuclei in total. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 13. A trophozoite of Entamoeba coli stained with trichrome is shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 14. A trophozoite of Entamoeba gingivalis from culture, stained with trichrome, is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 15. A cyst of Entamoeba hartmanni is shown in a wet mount stained with iodine. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 16. A cyst of Entamoeba hartmanni stained with trichrome is shown. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 17. A trophozoite of Entamoeba hartmanni stained with trichrome is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 18. A cyst of Entamoeba polecki in a wet mount stained with iodine is shown. Numerous chromatoid bodies are visible (indicated by arrows). This image is adapted from CDC materials. 19. A cyst of Entamoeba polecki stained with trichrome is shown. The large nucleus with a pleomorphic karyosome and numerous variably shaped chromatoid bodies are visible. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 20. A trophozoite of Entamoeba polecki stained with trichrome is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 21. A cyst of Endolimax nana in a direct wet mount stained with iodine is shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 22. A cyst of Endolimax nana stained with trichrome is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 23. A trophozoite of Endolimax nana stained with trichrome is shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 24. A cyst of Iodamoeba buetschlii from the same specimen as previous figures, stained with iodine, is shown. The glycogen vacuole is easily observed as a dark-staining mass within the cyst. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 25. A cyst of Iodamoeba buetschlii stained with trichrome is shown. Both the nucleus and the large glycogen vacuole are visible. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 26. A trophozoite of Iodamoeba buetschlii stained with trichrome is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 27. The egg of Capillaria philippinensis is shown in an unstained wet mount of stool. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 28. A cross-section of a gravid adult female Capillaria philippinensis from an intestinal biopsy specimen stained with H&E is shown. The bacillary band (blue arrow), intestine (red arrow), and uterus containing an egg in cross-section (black arrow) are visible. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 29. Amastigotes of Leishmania tropica are shown being released from a rupturing macrophage in an impression smear of a skin lesion biopsy. The patient had traveled to Egypt, Africa, and the Middle East. The species was identified as L. tropica based on culture in NNN medium and isoenzyme analysis. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 30. Leishmania mexicana amastigotes are shown lining the walls of two vacuoles in a biopsy specimen from a skin lesion stained with H&E. This arrangement is typical. The species was identified through culture and isoenzyme analysis. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 31. Promastigotes of Leishmania sp. from culture are depicted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 32. Microfilariae of Loa loa are shown at higher magnification (500x, oil). This image is adapted from CDC materials. 33. An adult Loa loa worm removed from the eye of a patient is shown. This image is courtesy of the Georgia State Public Health Laboratory and adapted from CDC resources. 34. A microfilaria of Brugia malayi in a thin blood smear stained with Giemsa is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 35. A microfilaria of Brugia timori in a thick blood smear from a patient in Indonesia, stained with Giemsa, is shown at 500x oil magnification. This image is courtesy of Dr. Thomas C. Orihel, Tulane University, and adapted from CDC resources. 36. A close-up of the posterior end of a Wuchereria bancrofti microfilaria is shown. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 37. Adult Wuchereria bancrofti worms are shown, with the male on the left and the female on the right. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 38. A microfilaria of Mansonella ozzardi in a thick blood smear stained with Giemsa is shown. The hook-like end of the tail is visible. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 39. A microfilaria of Mansonella perstans in a thick blood smear stained with Giemsa is depicted. This image is courtesy of the Parasitology Department, Public Health Lab, Ontario Agency for Health Protection and Promotion, Canada, and adapted from CDC resources. 40. A microfilaria of Mansonella streptocerca fixed in 2% formalin and stained with hematoxylin is shown. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 41. The scolex of Mesocestoides sp. stained with carmine is shown. Two suckers are clearly visible, and the lack of rostellar hooklets is noted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 42. A tetrathyridium of Mesocestoides sp. in the liver of a laboratory-infected mouse is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 43. An adult Metagonimus yokogawai fluke stained with carmine is shown. Labeled structures include the oral sucker (OS), pharynx (PH), intestine (IN), genitoacetabulum (GA), ovary (OV), paired testes (TE), and eggs within the uterus (EG). This image is adapted from CDC resources. 44. A snail of the genus Semisulcospira, an intermediate host of Metagonimus yokogawai, is depicted. This image is courtesy of Conchology, Inc., Mactan Island, Philippines, and adapted from CDC resources. 45. Spores of Encephalitozoon cuniculi in a kidney biopsy specimen stained with Ryan's modified trichrome are shown. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 46. Monoclonal antibody-based immunofluorescence identification of Encephalitozoon hellem is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 47. Encephalitozoon intestinalis spores stained with Calcofluor white are shown. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 48. Spores of Enterocytozoon bieneusi stained with Chromotrope 2R are depicted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 49. An adult Cuterebra sp., primarily a parasite of rodents and lagomorphs, is shown. Human infections are rare. This image is courtesy of the Georgia Museum of Natural History, University of Georgia, and adapted from CDC resources. 50. An adult Dermatobia hominis, the human bot fly, is depicted. This image is courtesy of the Georgia Museum of Natural History, University of Georgia, and adapted from CDC resources. 51. A first instar larva of Oestrus ovis collected from the eye of a patient in India presenting with conjunctivitis is shown. This image is courtesy of the LV Prasad Eye Institute, Banjara Hills, India, and adapted from CDC resources. 52. A close-up of the posterior spiracles of the Oestrus ovis larva is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC materials. 53. The egg of Oesophagostomum sp. in an unstained wet mount of stool is shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 54. The tail-end of an Oesophagostomum sp. L3 infective larva is shown. The long tail space and tapering tail sheath are visible. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 55. Adult Oesophagostomum sp. worms are shown, with the bursa (BU) visible. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 56. A higher magnification (200x) of Oesophagostomum sp. in tissue specimens shows large platy myarian muscle cells (MU) and a thick, muscled esophagus (ES). This image is adapted from CDC resources. 57. Microfilariae of Onchocerca volvulus from a skin nodule of a patient from Zambia, stained with H&E, are shown at 1000x oil magnification. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 58. Microfilariae of Onchocerca volvulus within the uterus of an adult female are depicted. The specimen was taken from the same patient as the previous image. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 59. A cross-section of an adult female Onchocerca volvulus stained with H&E shows numerous microfilariae within the uterus. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 60. A cross-section of an adult female Onchocerca sp. from a scalp nodule biopsy of a patient from Liberia is shown. The intestine (blue arrow), uterine tubes (red arrows), and cuticular nodules (green arrows) are visible. The weak musculature under the thick cuticle is also noted. This image is courtesy of Drs. Philip LeBoit and Paul Borbeau and adapted from CDC resources. 61. An adult Opisthorchis felineus is depicted. This image is courtesy of the Web Atlas of Medical Parasitology and the Korean Society for Parasitology and adapted from CDC resources. 62. A common intermediate host of Opisthorchis spp. is shown. This image is courtesy of Michal Manas and adapted from CDC resources. 63. The egg of Opisthorchis viverrini in an unstained wet mount of concentrated stool is shown at 400x magnification. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 64. An adult Opisthorchis viverrini is depicted. This image is courtesy of the Web Atlas of Medical Parasitology and the Korean Society for Parasitology and adapted from CDC resources. 65. The egg of Paragonimus westermani in an unstained wet mount is shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 66. The egg of Paragonimus sp. from a lung biopsy stained with H&E is shown. The egg measures 80–90 µm by 40–45 µm. The species was not identified in this case. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 67. A higher magnification (1000x, oil) of Paragonimus kellicotti eggs is shown. This image is courtesy of Dr. Gary Procop and adapted from CDC resources. 68. Sections of several adult Paragonimus kellicotti worms from a pleural biopsy stained with H&E are shown. The integument is absent in most worms, likely due to an old infection, but remnants of the gonad and uterine tubes are visible. This image is courtesy of Dr. Miguel Madariaga, University of Nebraska Medical Center, and adapted from CDC resources. 69. An adult Pediculus humanus (head or body louse) is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 70. An empty shell of a nit (egg) of Pediculus humanus is shown. The nymph has already hatched. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 71. A trophozoite of Pentatrichomonas hominis in a stool specimen stained with iron hematoxylin is shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 72. A close-up of the anterior end of Philophthalmus spp. adult flukes shows the oral sucker (OS), pharynx (PH), and acetabulum (AC). This image is adapted from CDC resources. 73. A snail intermediate host of Philophthalmus spp. is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 74. Trophozoites of Pneumocystis jirovecii in a bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) specimen from an AIDS patient stained with Giemsa are shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 75. Cysts of Pneumocystis jirovecii in lung tissue stained with methenamine silver and H&E are shown. The cyst walls are stained black, but the intracystic bodies are not visible with this stain. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 76. Direct immunofluorescence antibody staining using monoclonal antibodies targeting Pneumocystis jirovecii is shown. The image is from a BAL specimen of a patient with malignancy. This image is courtesy of Brigham & Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, and adapted from CDC resources. 77. A trophozoite of Retortamonas intestinalis in a stool specimen stained with trichrome is shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 78. A cyst of Retortamonas intestinalis in a stool specimen stained with trichrome is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 79. A sporulated oocyst of Sarcocystis sp. in unstained wet mounts at 400x magnification is shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 80. A sporulated oocyst of Sarcocystis sp. in a wet mount viewed under differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy at 400x magnification is shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 81. An individual sporocyst of Sarcocystis sp. in a wet mount viewed under UV microscopy at 400x magnification is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 82. A higher magnification (1000x) of a Sarcocystis sarcocyst shows numerous bradyzoites. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 83. The egg of Schistosoma haematobium in a wet mount of a urine concentrate is shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 84. The egg of Schistosoma intercalatum in a wet mount is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 85. The egg of Schistosoma japonicum in an unstained wet mount is shown. Small, inconspicuous spines are visible (indicated by red arrows). This image is adapted from CDC resources. 86. The egg of Schistosoma japonicum in an unstained wet mount of stool is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 87. Adult Schistosoma mansoni worms are shown, with the thin female residing in the gynecophoral canal of the thicker male. The tuberculate exterior of the male is noted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 88. The egg of Schistosoma mekongi is shown, with an inconspicuous spine (indicated by a red arrow). This image is adapted from CDC resources. 89. A proliferating sparganum in groin tissue of a patient from Paraguay, stained with H&E, is shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 90. A higher magnification of a sparganum in lung tissue shows calcareous corpuscles (indicated by green arrows). This image is adapted from CDC resources. 91. A sparganum removed from the ocular conjunctiva of a patient from Taiwan is shown. The worm measured 40 mm in length. This image is courtesy of Dr. John H. Cross and the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences, Bethesda, MD, and adapted from CDC resources. 92. A rhabditiform larva of Strongyloides stercoralis in an unstained wet mount of stool is shown. The genital primordium (blue arrow), rhabditoid esophagus (red arrow), and short buccal canal (green arrow) are visible. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 93. A higher magnification (1000x oil) of a third-stage filariform larva of Strongyloides stercoralis shows a notched tail. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 94. An adult free-living female Strongyloides stercoralis is shown, with a row of eggs visible within the female’s body. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 95. A longitudinal section of a larva of Strongyloides stercoralis from the same specimen as previous figures is shown at 400x magnification. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 96. An unstained egg of Taenia sp. teased from a proglottid of an adult is shown. Four hooks are clearly visible. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 97. The scolex of Taenia saginata is shown, with four large suckers and no rostellum or rostellar hooks. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 98. A proglottid of Taenia sp. injected with India ink demonstrates the number of primary uterine branches (>12). This image is courtesy of the Oregon State Public Health Laboratory and adapted from CDC resources. 99. A close-up of a cross-section of a Taenia sp. proglottid stained with H&E shows numerous calcareous corpuscles. This image is courtesy of Ameripath and adapted from CDC resources. 100. An adult Taenia saginata worm is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 101. The posterior end of a female Thelazia sp. is shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 102. The intermediate host of Thelazia spp., Musca domestica (the house fly), is depicted. This species has been implicated in the transmission of thelaziasis in the United States and Asia. This image is courtesy of the Parasite and Diseases Image Library, Australia, and adapted from CDC resources. 103. A larva of Toxocara canis is shown hatching. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 104. A close-up of the posterior end of an adult Toxocara cati worm is depicted. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 105. Encysted larvae of Trichinella in tissue stained with H&E are shown. The nucleated stichocyte (ST), prominent lateral chords or bacillary bands (LC), immature reproductive tubes (RT), and intestine (IN) are visible. The image was captured at 1000x magnification and adapted from CDC resources. 106. A higher magnification of Trichinella larvae in tongue tissue of a rat stained with H&E is shown. This image was captured at 400x magnification and adapted from CDC resources. 107. A larva of Trichinella liberated from bear meat is depicted. This larva is from a different case than those shown in previous figures. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 108. The egg of Trichostrongylus sp. in an unstained wet mount of stool is shown. This image is courtesy of the Indiana State Department of Health and adapted from CDC resources. 109. The egg of a trichostrongyle from the same specimen as previous figures is shown. A developing larva can be observed within the egg. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 110. The posterior end of a male Trichostrongylus sp. is shown, with the bursa (red arrow) and spicule (blue arrow) visible. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 111. A close-up of the eggs from a Tunga penetrans specimen is shown. This image is adapted from CDC resources. 112. Cross-sections of Tunga penetrans in tissue stained with H&E are shown. The labeled structures include the cuticle (CU), gut (GU), and developing eggs (EG). This image is adapted from CDC resources.
